Customer Segmentation Project¶

Segmenting customers based on behavior and demographics using K-Means clustering, to enable targeted marketing and personalized business strategy.

Approach: Load customer data → explore it → scale features → find the optimal number of clusters (Elbow + Silhouette methods) → run K-Means → visualize and profile each segment → assign business-friendly names to each segment.

1. Setup & Imports¶

In [1]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

sns.set_style("whitegrid")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)

2. Load the Data¶

The dataset contains 515 customers with demographic and behavioral attributes:

Column Description
CustomerID Unique customer identifier
Age Customer age
Gender Customer gender
Annual_Income_Lakhs Annual income (₹ Lakhs)
Spending_Score Score (1–100) assigned based on spending behavior
Purchase_Frequency Number of orders placed per year
Recency_Days Days since the customer's last purchase
Preferred_Category Product category the customer buys most

4. Feature Scaling¶

K-Means is distance-based, so features on different scales (e.g. Age in years vs Income in Lakhs) must be standardized before clustering, otherwise high-magnitude features would dominate the distance calculation.

In [7]:
features = ["Age", "Annual_Income_Lakhs", "Spending_Score", "Purchase_Frequency", "Recency_Days"]
X = df[features].copy()

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
X_scaled = pd.DataFrame(X_scaled, columns=features)
X_scaled.head()

5. Finding the Optimal Number of Clusters¶

Two standard techniques are used together:

  • Elbow Method — plots inertia (within-cluster variance) vs k; look for the point where the drop levels off
  • Silhouette Score — measures how well-separated the clusters are (higher is better, range -1 to 1)
In [8]:
inertias = []
silhouettes = []
K_range = range(2, 10)

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X_scaled)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(list(K_range), inertias, marker="o", color="#2F5CE0")
axes[0].set_title("Elbow Method")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Number of Clusters (k)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Inertia")

axes[1].plot(list(K_range), silhouettes, marker="o", color="#1E8E5A")
axes[1].set_title("Silhouette Score by k")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Number of Clusters (k)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Silhouette Score")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("plots/04_elbow_silhouette.png", bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

best_k = list(K_range)[int(np.argmax(silhouettes))]
print(f"Best k by silhouette score: {best_k}")

Best k by silhouette score: 5

6. Fit Final K-Means Model¶

Based on the elbow and silhouette results, we fit the final model with the chosen number of clusters and assign each customer to a segment.

In [9]:
k = best_k  # chosen from the analysis above
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
df["Cluster"] = kmeans.fit_predict(X_scaled)

print(f"Number of segments: {k}")
df["Cluster"].value_counts().sort_index()

Number of segments: 5

9. Naming the Segments¶

Based on the average characteristics of each cluster, we assign business-friendly names. This step is manual/interpretive — a data scientist looks at the profile table above and translates numbers into a segment story that a marketing team can act on.

Update the segment_names dictionary below to match the clusters your run actually produces (cluster numbers can vary run to run).

In [15]:
# Inspect the profile table above, then map each cluster number to a name.
# Example logic: high income + high spending -> "Premium Loyalists", etc.
segment_profile_sorted = segment_profile.sort_values("Spending_Score", ascending=False)
print(segment_profile_sorted)

segment_names = {}
for cluster_id, row in segment_profile.iterrows():
    if row["Annual_Income_Lakhs"] > segment_profile["Annual_Income_Lakhs"].median() and row["Spending_Score"] > segment_profile["Spending_Score"].median():
        segment_names[cluster_id] = "Premium Loyalists"
    elif row["Annual_Income_Lakhs"] > segment_profile["Annual_Income_Lakhs"].median() and row["Spending_Score"] <= segment_profile["Spending_Score"].median():
        segment_names[cluster_id] = "Affluent Disengaged"
    elif row["Annual_Income_Lakhs"] <= segment_profile["Annual_Income_Lakhs"].median() and row["Spending_Score"] > segment_profile["Spending_Score"].median():
        segment_names[cluster_id] = "Budget Enthusiasts"
    elif row["Recency_Days"] > segment_profile["Recency_Days"].median():
        segment_names[cluster_id] = "Price-Sensitive / At Risk"
    else:
        segment_names[cluster_id] = "Steady Regulars"

df["Segment_Name"] = df["Cluster"].map(segment_names)
segment_profile["Segment_Name"] = segment_profile.index.map(segment_names)
segment_profile

Business Interpretation (example — adapt to your actual output)¶

  • Premium Loyalists — high income, high spending, frequent buyers → prioritize retention (loyalty programs, early access to new products)
  • Affluent Disengaged — high income but low engagement → win-back campaigns, personalized offers to re-activate
  • Budget Enthusiasts — lower income but high spending score → value-driven promotions, bundle deals
  • Price-Sensitive / At Risk — infrequent, high recency (haven't purchased recently) → discount-led re-engagement, reminder emails
  • Steady Regulars — moderate across the board → maintain consistent engagement, upsell opportunities

(Exact labels depend on the cluster numbers your run produces — see the printed segment_profile_sorted table above to map cluster IDs to the correct story.)
